title: The Principles of the Truth-O-Meter: PolitiFact's methodology for independent fact-checking

extracted.subtask_short: Rating a political claim's accuracy on a graded scale
extracted.subtask_description: Selecting checkable claims, researching them against primary sources and speaker input, and converting the resulting evidentiary assessment into a discrete, graded Truth-O-Meter rating via multi-editor vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability threshold with hyperbole license
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold question: "Is the statement rooted in a fact that is verifiable?" Statements of pure opinion, or predictions about the future that cannot yet be checked, are explicitly excluded. The methodology also builds in "license for hyperbole" for political rhetoric — obvious figures of speech are not treated as factual claims to be checked literally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance filter for checkable claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should be one that would, if wrong, actually mislead people — trivial misstatements or slips of the tongue are deprioritized in favor of claims that are substantively "misleading or sound wrong."

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach filter — likelihood of being repeated
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority goes to statements "likely to be passed on and repeated by others" — i.e., claims with viral or rhetorical potential, since the harm of an unchecked false claim scales with how far it spreads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest test
rubrics_metrics.description: The operational heuristic used by editors: "Would a typical person hear or read the statement and wonder: Is that true?" If the claim wouldn't provoke that reaction, it's not a priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact the speaker for basis of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters attempt to reach the original speaker (or their office/campaign) to ask for the basis of the claim and any supporting evidence — this mirrors the "right of reply" step also found in Full Fact's process and gives the claimant a chance to substantiate before independent research proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check prior fact-checks of the same or similar claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters review whether the same or a similar claim has already been fact-checked (by PolitiFact or elsewhere), to build on established findings rather than duplicate effort or contradict a previous verdict without cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert consultation across multiple experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters consult multiple subject-matter experts, deliberately not relying on a single expert's framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for primary sources and original documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The methodology explicitly states a preference for "primary sources and original documentation" over second-hand accounts or another outlet's paraphrase of the underlying document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from the claimant's own framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a campaign or speaker provides supporting material, PolitiFact does its own independent verification rather than accepting the claimant's characterization of that material at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six-point Truth-O-Meter graded support scale
rubrics_metrics.description: TRUE: "The statement is accurate and there's nothing significant missing." MOSTLY TRUE: "The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information." HALF TRUE: "The statement is partially accurate but leaves out important details or takes things out of context." MOSTLY FALSE: "The statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression." FALSE: "The statement is not accurate." PANTS ON FIRE: "The statement is not accurate and makes a ridiculous claim." The top three bands are all "accurate" but differentiated purely by completeness and context; the bottom two bands are differentiated purely by the rhetorical extremity of the false claim, not by any additional factual criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof is on the speaker; default skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "The burden of proof is on the speaker" — the default posture is skeptical; a claim is not assumed supportable unless evidence for it can be found or supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate based on information known at the time, not hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are rated based on the information known at the time the statement was made, not with the benefit of hindsight — a claim that was reasonable given contemporaneous evidence is not penalized for later being overtaken by new facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-editor vote on final rating
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter who researches a claim proposes a rating to an assigning editor. That proposed rating and the underlying research are then reviewed by additional editors who probe specific questions: is the statement literally true or false; are there alternative reasonable interpretations of what the speaker meant; what evidence did the speaker have available at the time; and how does this claim compare to precedent. Three editors vote on the final rating, with two votes deciding.
